A similar > repository name or copied README does not establish that a download is official.




Join the Reverse Engineering Community
Discord · Q&A · Show and Tell

--- See a feature in an app that you want in your own product? Ask your agent to investigate it with REA. It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project. REA connects your agent to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites. You can also use the same tools from your terminal. Analysis runs locally, and results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion. Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions. Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval. Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine. > **[Visit the REA website](https://rea.tools/)** for setup instructions, illustrated guides, and real case studies. ## Quick start On Linux, Ghidra, JADX, firmware tool launches and static JavaScript/Electron analysis require a procps-compatible system `ps` for process ownership checks. Recovery steps are in `docs/getting-started/installation.md` under "Linux owned-process prerequisite". ### Set up your agent With Node.js and npm installed, run: ```bash npx rea-agents setup ``` Choose your agents, review the proposed changes, and approve them. Setup adds REA's MCP server and matching workflow instructions, with backups of existing configuration. Restart your agent afterward. Setup records the selected runtime and REA entry script directly. If acquired through a package runner, keep its cache entry available. Run package acquisition from a trusted directory outside the target project. Installation and recovery details are in the setup guide below. Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and [other agents](docs/getting-started/installation.md#supported-agents). See [installation and setup](docs/getting-started/installation.md) for provider configuration, manual MCP registration, Claude Code/Codex plugins, and the Cursor Marketplace plugin. MCP advertises compact input schemas to reduce context overhead; guidance a compact schema omits follows the tool description. The full tool set and canonical server validation are unchanged. See "Compact input schema profile" in the MCP contracts guide. Output schemas are omitted from `tools/list` by default: no model API reads them, and REA validates every result itself. Set `REA_MCP_OUTPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=compact` to advertise each output schema within a 4,096-byte budget. Both settings keep canonical server-side validation and complete structured results. See "Output schemas" in the MCP contracts guide. ### Ask your agent ```text Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a similar feature for my project. ``` Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand. ### Use the terminal Inspect an extracted JavaScript/Electron app directory or ASAR: ```bash npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json ``` The result includes modules, imports, Electron boundaries and their evidence. Replace the path with your target, such as `"D:/apps/example"` on Windows. To install the `rea` command for regular use: ```bash npm install --global rea-agents rea --help ``` For native analysis, configure a provider first. See the [CLI and Evidence guide](docs/getting-started/cli.md) for native commands, provider selection, snapshots and scripting. ### Update REA REA changes quickly, and new releases include frequent bug fixes. Keep your installation up to date. For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`: ```bash rea update ``` `rea --update` is an alias for this verified workflow and accepts the same global output flags. Use `rea update` when combining it with other command controls. Updater commands retain at most 4 MiB of stdout and stderr combined. Oversized metadata replies are rejected after the command exits; verbose installs continue with bounded diagnostics. Human progress output respects terminal backpressure and waits for submitted writes to finish. Bun global updates require Bun 1.2.17 or later. With an older Bun release, upgrade Bun manually before running `rea update`. To refresh your agent registrations and skill, run the setup command printed by the update. If you use `npx`, update your agent setup with: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` Review the setup changes and restart your agent. For one-off CLI commands, use `npx rea-agents@latest` followed by the command. With Bun, use `bunx rea-agents@latest` in place of `npx rea-agents@latest`. ## How REA works Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code. REA returns findings with their evidence. The agent uses them to ask follow-up questions, explain the behavior, or write and test an implementation. CLI commands use the same workflows. ![REA investigation flow: your agent asks about a local target, REA inspects and traces it using analysis tools, and the agent uses the returned code, references and unknowns to explain, implement and test.](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg) [Open the full-size figure](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg). ## What you can analyze REA requires Node.js 22.x (>=22.23.4), 24.x (>=24.22.1), or 26.12.1+, plus npm. Additional tools and host support depend on the target: | Target | What REA returns | Requirements and guide | | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Desktop installations | Runtime candidates, supporting files, component markers and next probes | Built-in bounded directory/header inspection; [desktop applications](docs/desktop-applications.md) | | Native binaries | Pseudocode, assembly, strings, symbols, calls and references | Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna; [native analysis](docs/guides/native/native-investigation.md) | | Offline ELF layout | Sections, segments, original symbols/relocations and static mitigation candidates | Caller-supplied pwntools on Linux x64; [binary diagnostics](docs/guides/native/binary-diagnostics.md) | | Go binaries | Embedded compiler version, modules, replacements and build settings | Built-in static ELF/PE/thin Mach-O inspection; no Go installation required | | GPU code objects | CUDA/HIP targets, selected kernel parameters and resources, retained PTX text | Built-in static ELF/PE/fatbin/CUBIN/PTX inspection; [GPU code objects](docs/gpu-code-objects.md) | | Model artifacts | GGUF / safetensors metadata, tensor declarations and derived totals | Built-in header inspection; optional full-file hash; [model files](docs/model-artifacts.md) | | IL2CPP metadata | Unity global-metadata.dat assembly images, type and method names and index ranges | Built-in static decoding of versions 24, 27, 29, 31 and 39; no Unity required | | Godot PCK | Archive inventory and extraction, original header/directory facts and selected content identities | Built-in static formats 2, 3 and 4; no Godot required | | Rust binaries | Embedded cargo-auditable crate names, versions, sources and dependency edges | Built-in static ELF/PE/thin Mach-O inspection; [Rust binaries](docs/rust-binaries.md) | | PE certificates | Authenticode WIN_CERTIFICATE entries and PKCS#7 signer/X.509 identity fields | Built-in static PE inspection; [PE certificates](docs/pe-certificates.md) | | PE imports | Import and delay-load DLL names, ordinals, IAT RVAs and pefile import hash | Built-in static PE inspection; [PE imports](docs/pe-imports.md) | | Windows shortcuts | Shell Link target, arguments, working dir, ExtraData and Tracker droid facts | Built-in static LNK inspection; [Windows shortcuts](docs/guides/native/windows-shortcut.md) | | ELF notes | PT_NOTE/SHT_NOTE owners, types, GNU build-id and ABI-tag fields | Built-in static ELF inspection; [ELF notes](docs/elf-notes.md) | | DWARF compile units | Compile-unit name, directory, producer, language, and dwo_name | Built-in static ELF, Mach-O, and PE inspection; [DWARF compile units](docs/guides/native/dwarf-units.md) | | ELF dependencies | DT_NEEDED, SONAME, RPATH/RUNPATH, GNU versions, and undefined imports | Built-in static ELF inspection; [ELF dependencies](docs/elf-dependencies.md) | | Binary hardening | PIE, NX, RELRO, CFG and related header flags for ELF, PE and Mach-O | Built-in static header inspection; [binary hardening](docs/binary-hardening.md) | | Apple IPS crashes | .ips metadata, threads, images, registers and documented crash classes | Built-in static JSON inspection; [Apple IPS](docs/apple-ips.md) | | Linux kernel modules | .modinfo keys, __versions CRCs, this_module presence, and signature trailer | Built-in static ELF inspection; [kernel modules](docs/kernel-modules.md) | | Erlang BEAM | IFF chunks, atoms, exports, imports, lambdas and the Code header | Built-in static BEAM inspection; [Erlang BEAM](docs/erlang-beam.md) | | NuGet packages | Package identity, dependency groups, license, repository and ZIP contents | Built-in static .nupkg inspection; [NuGet packages](docs/guides/managed/nuget-nupkg.md) | | WASM artifact | Validation, sections, exact import/export WAT forms and decoded WAT | Caller-supplied WABT 1.0.42; `inspect_wasm_artifact` | | EVM bytecode | Dispatch selectors, byte offsets, inferred arguments and mutability | Local raw/hex carrier on Linux x64; [offline EVM guide](docs/guides/evm/evm-bytecode.md) | | SQLite databases | Tables, columns, indexes, views, triggers and selected ordinary-table rows | Local database/WAL snapshot; Node.js 24.x >=24.15 or 26+ with native SQLite limits | | Recorded Linux crashes | Raw notes, every recorded thread's registers/signals and optional mapping candidates | Caller-supplied pwntools on Linux x64; optional GDB/pwndbg; [recorded crashes](docs/guides/native/recorded-crashes.md) | | JavaScript / Electron | Modules, imports, source maps, routes, IPC, native add-ons, `rea audit-release-exposure` | Node.js and npm; Linux: procps-compatible `ps`; [application analysis](docs/guides/javascript/javascript-application-workflows.md) | | Websites | Page structure, scripts, network observations and requested screenshots | A Chrome-family browser; [browser analysis](docs/guides/web/browser-observation.md) | | Saved network captures | Requests, responses, exposed payloads and source locations | HAR or Fiddler Everywhere SAZ; mitmdump on Linux for native mitmproxy; [capture guide](docs/guides/web/web-network-captures.md) | | .NET assemblies | Metadata, CIL instructions, declared native dependencies and build comparisons | None (static only); [managed-code guide](docs/guides/managed/managed-code-analysis.md) | | Android APKs | Manifest declarations, classes, decompiled methods and references | Headless JADX and a full JDK on Linux/macOS/Windows x64; [Android guide](docs/guides/android/android-analysis.md) | | APK signatures | v1/v2/v3/v3.1 signers, certificate fingerprints, key rotation and digest self-consistency | None (static only); `inspect_apk_signature` | | Android devices | Devices, packages, processes, logs, dumps, screen captures, and APK/file transfers | Caller-supplied adb (emulator or hardware); [ADB guide](docs/guides/android/adb-device-analysis.md) | | JEB projects | Engine-backed project units, artifact digests and type/method pseudo-code | A caller-started JEB client serving MCP, selected with REA_JEB_MCP_URL; [JEB guide](docs/providers/jeb-analysis.md) | | Android resources | Decoded manifest, string tables, locales and version facts | Caller-supplied Apktool launcher; [resource guide](docs/guides/android/apktool-resource-analysis.md) | | Flutter apps | Dart snapshot hash, per-ABI library digests and engine build provenance | None (static APK parsing); [Flutter guide](docs/guides/android/flutter-analysis.md) | | Firmware | Regions, extraction results and native-analysis handoffs | Binwalk / Unblob on Linux; [firmware guide](docs/guides/firmware/firmware-analysis.md) | | Recorded packets | Selected fields, repeated values, filters and decode-as rules | Linux: TShark 4.x + prlimit; [capture guide](docs/guides/data/packet-captures.md) | | Packet summaries | Endpoints, DNS, TLS SNI, protocol distribution and HTTP requests | Caller-supplied tshark and capinfos (Linux-verified); [pcap guide](docs/guides/data/pcap-analysis.md) | | Recorded logic signals | Decoder annotations, sample ranges and diagnostics | Linux: sigrok-cli 0.7.2 + prlimit; [signal recordings](docs/guides/signals/signal-recordings.md) | | Packages and resources | File inventories, digests, plists, Apple bundle anatomy and extracted resources | [Artifact and JavaScript guide](docs/guides/javascript/javascript-artifact-reconstruction.md), [Apple applications](docs/guides/apple/apple-application-analysis.md) | | Process behavior | Terminal output, interactions, exit and filesystem observations, and run comparisons | Linux/macOS with a native PTY; [process capture](docs/guides/runtime/process-capture.md) | | PyInstaller executables | CArchive members, Python version, entry scripts and extracted bytecode | None (static only); [Python packaged applications](docs/python-packaged-applications.md) | | Deno compile binaries | Virtual files, entry point, recorded options, npm snapshot length | None (static only); [Deno compile executables](docs/deno-standalone.md) | Static JavaScript and .NET inspection read the supplied files without running the application. Runtime capture runs or interacts with the selected target using your user permissions; each runtime guide describes its effects. For offline native-binary inspection, REA also supports caller-supplied GNU objdump and Rizin. See the [reverse-engineering tools guide](docs/reverse-engineering-tools.md) for provider setup, CLI commands, and Evidence limitations. REA does not install or update either provider. Native formats and host support vary by provider. See [Hopper and Ghidra setup](docs/getting-started/installation.md#hopper), the [IDA guide](docs/providers/ida-provider.md) (including an optional native MCP bridge), the [Kuna decompiler guide](docs/kuna-provider.md), and [experimental Windows Ghidra support](docs/providers/windows-ghidra-p0.md). Ghidra also supports [16-bit DOS analysis](docs/providers/ghidra-dos.md). For large binaries, raise the provider's startup deadline with `REA_GHIDRA_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS` or `REA_HOPPER_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS`. For provider selection, see the [CLI guide](docs/getting-started/cli.md#choose-a-provider). Check [release availability](docs/getting-started/installation.md#released-package-and-main) for features added since the latest npm release. ## Showcases ### DX-Ball: reconstruct a sound-pan calculation Follow a sound call into its position-to-pan helper, inspect the instructions, and turn incomplete pseudocode into C. The reconstruction passes 3,205 original-x86 cases and reproduces all 63 compiled function bytes. [Read the case study](https://rea.tools/showcase/dx-ball/) · [Reconstruction repository](https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/dx-ball) ### Notion: trace the Electron clipboard bridge Find the renderer's clipboard API, follow it through preload and IPC into the main process, and inspect the rich clipboard format. [Read the case study](https://rea.tools/showcase/notion/) ### TH04: recover a DOS bullet-ring calculation Inspect the original PC-98 game's 16-bit instructions, recover the fixed and aimed angle calculations, and compare the reconstructed C++ with the historical compiler output. [Read the case study](https://rea.tools/showcase/th04/) · [Reconstruction repository](https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/th04) ### Build RL environments with REA Record a web app session, turn its API into tools, and export an environment an AI agent can use. Run it with AgentEnv, then add tasks and reward checks for RL training or evaluation. [Read the guide](https://rea.tools/guides/rl-environments/) · [Watch the video](https://x.com/reatools/status/2112574822584918075?s=20) If you've used REA on something interesting, we'd love to see it. Share your case in an [issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) or a [pull request](https://github.com/morluto/rea/pulls), including the target, your question, how REA helped, and what you found. ## Build RL environments Give an AI agent a local environment to practice tasks such as finding an issue or creating a folder, without running the original app. Use it for reinforcement learning (RL) or to test how well an agent completes tasks. REA turns recorded API requests and responses into tools the agent can call. The environment uses the recorded data and supports changes only when the recording confirms their effects. With REA set up in your agent, replace the example URL and folder tasks below with your own: ```text Use REA to build an RL environment from my test web app at http://127.0.0.1:3000. Cover listing, creating, renaming, and deleting folders. You may create and remove test folders. Leave existing data unchanged. Save it in a folder named my-env. Check which operations work and tell me how to run it. ```
Use the command line instead Use these commands if you already have a file containing the app’s recorded browser requests and responses. Running the result also requires AgentEnv and Docker. ```sh rea environment-build ./session.har ./my-env --name my-env --json agent-env run ./my-env ```
REA exports a runnable environment with a basic test to check that it starts and responds. Use it with your RL framework to define task goals, add reward checks, and run training. [Build an environment](https://rea.tools/guides/rl-environments/) · [Environment reference](docs/agent-environments.md) · [Watch the demo on X](https://x.com/reatools/status/2112574822584918075?s=20) ### Desktop app environments REA can also build an environment of a Linux desktop app, which an agent uses through screenshots, the mouse and the keyboard. From a one-line request, such as "Build me a Gnote environment where the agent adds olive oil to the shopping list note", your agent installs the app on a local build computer, writes the task, exports the environment and checks the task in a fresh computer. The machine that builds it needs Linux on amd64 or arm64, Docker and the agentenv framework version the guide pins. [Set up desktop app environments](docs/desktop-build-computer.md) ## FAQ
Which agents can use REA? Any agent that supports local MCP servers. Setup configures the [supported agents](docs/getting-started/installation.md#supported-agents); other clients can use [manual MCP registration](docs/getting-started/installation.md#mcp-registry).
Do I need a native analysis engine? Deep native analysis uses Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna, depending on the target and operation. Static JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native analysis engine. Setup can install Hopper after approval; Ghidra, IDA and Kuna use your existing installations. See [provider setup](docs/getting-started/installation.md#hopper) for the options and their supported targets.
Do I need to start Hopper first? REA starts Hopper when an operation needs it. On macOS, a first-run dialog may ask you to choose demo mode or activate your license. Complete that prompt in the same user session before your first CLI/MCP operation or unattended job. Open Hopper manually if needed. See [Hopper startup and troubleshooting](docs/getting-started/installation.md#launcher-paths-and-troubleshooting).
What does installing the skill from skills.sh do? The skill supplies investigation instructions for your agent. Use `npx rea-agents setup` to register REA's MCP server and install the matching instructions, then restart your agent. See [skill-only installation](docs/getting-started/installation.md#skill-only-installation).
What code does REA return? Native analysis returns pseudocode and assembly. JavaScript/Electron analysis recovers modules and their relationships. Your agent uses these findings to write and test an implementation; the [showcases](#showcases) give worked examples.
Does REA upload my app? REA analyzes targets locally. Your agent receives the tool results, and its model provider has its own data policy.
What should I do if I hit a bug? Update first; a recent release may already fix it. For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`: ```bash rea update ``` For agent setup through `npx`: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` If you're using an agent, complete the [setup refresh](#update-rea) and restart it. Retry the same task. If the problem persists, [open an issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) with your REA version, target type, steps to reproduce and error output.
## Documentation Start with the website's [worked guides](https://rea.tools/guides/). For exact options, prerequisites and result contracts: - [Installation and setup](docs/getting-started/installation.md): agent registration, provider configuration, updates and uninstall. - [Readiness and troubleshooting](docs/getting-started/installation.md#check-readiness-for-your-task): diagnose one agent or analysis engine. - [CLI and Evidence](docs/getting-started/cli.md): commands, provider selection, snapshots, import/export and exit statuses. - [MCP contracts](docs/reference/mcp-contracts.md) and [agent prompts](docs/getting-started/mcp-prompts.md): tool results, sessions and guided investigations. - [Tool catalog](docs/reference/mcp-contracts.md#generated-catalog): generated inventory of tools, providers and CLI commands. - [Roadmap](docs/development/roadmap.md): planned work and capability trackers. Report vulnerabilities through [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). ## Star history 🎉 **400,000 GitHub stars — thank you!** Thanks to everyone using REA, reporting bugs, requesting features, testing builds, and contributing fixes. ## Disclaimer See [DISCLAIMER.md](DISCLAIMER.md) for responsible-use guidance. The project's position on illegal or unauthorized use covers all REA versions, distribution channels, and platforms; each copy retains its applicable licenses. REA is for lawful research, education, interoperability, software preservation, and analysis of software you own or are authorized to examine. ## Contributing We'd love your help with REA! [Open an issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) to report a bug or suggest a feature, or [send a pull request](https://github.com/morluto/rea/pulls) to improve the code or docs. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for development setup and checks, [testing](docs/development/testing.md) for verification lanes, and the [architecture map](docs/architecture/architecture.mermaid) for selected layers and dependency paths. ## License [MIT](LICENSE) REA-authored code is licensed under MIT. Third-party material retains its own licenses and copyright notices; see [Third-party notices](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md) for the dependency inventory, preserved license texts, and external-tool terms. **You must legally obtain and be authorized to use commercial tools**, including IDA Pro / Hex-Rays decompilers, Hopper, and JEB, under their applicable licenses. REA grants no tool license, key, or activation entitlement. Trials and demos remain subject to vendor terms, including user, feature, automation, and output sharing restrictions. Cracked copies, stolen keys, unauthorized key sharing, and bypassing license restrictions are not authorized. This guidance does not amend MIT or third-party licenses.

/ jitterRatio。将这三项嵌套在 backoff:{} 中， 调度器读到 undefined，于是 undefined \* 2ⁿ = NaN，而持久会话日志会直接拒绝非有限数值—— 一个本可恢复的瞬时故障因此导致整轮对话报废。应返回已解析完毕的扁平策略。 **一次被中断的工具调用会永久污染该会话。** 缺少对应结果的工具调用在重放时，上游返回 400 ## 💡 What is Univer?

**Univer** is an Office SDK for building Office applications inside your own product. It provides Office editing, calculation, collaboration, and file processing for people and existing agents, using your data and permissions. The product family covers spreadsheets, documents, presentations, relational tables, canvases, and PDFs.

Univer Office SDK has three parts: - **Web SDK** is the foundation: content models, editing, rendering, formula calculation, and Facade APIs (application-facing APIs). Compose its plugins into an embedded editor or your own Office application, and reuse the content models, commands, and calculation for Headless processing without an interactive editor. - **Server SDK** adds backend services for real-time collaboration, edit history, and Office file import and export. - **AI SDK** connects Office capabilities to existing agents and workflows, with content tools, execution, and review integrations. **This repository provides the Web SDK's core architecture and engine implementations under Apache-2.0**: content models and snapshot formats, plugin and dependency management, the command system, formula and rendering engines, Facade APIs, UI foundation, and Sheets and Docs editing capabilities. Commercial Web SDK plugins, Server SDK, and commercial AI SDK extensions are distributed and licensed separately. Agents can use the same open-source APIs; your application supplies the model and tool orchestration. The [quotation example](#connect-your-application-to-editable-content) demonstrates editing, calculation, and saving without an AI SDK dependency. ### Open-source capabilities
Area Selected capabilities
Sheets · Editing and layout Cell styles, merged cells, in-cell rich text, freeze panes, floating images, and undo/redo.
Sheets · Data and calculation Formulas, defined names, filtering, sorting, data validation, conditional formatting, hyperlinks, comments, and find and replace.
Docs Rich-text editing, paragraph formatting, lists, hyperlinks, comments, and drawing integration.
Features are composed through plugins and presets; the [quick start](#quick-start) uses only the **Sheets Core preset**. Images use the corresponding drawing plugins. See the [feature comparison](https://univer.ai/compare/) for detailed open-source and commercial coverage. The demos below showcase the wider **Univer Office SDK**, including commercial capabilities. They show more than the default open-source setup; see [open source and commercial extensions](#open-source-and-commercial-extensions) for scope.

## 🚀 Build on the open-source foundation

Your goal Use the open-source foundation Start here
Embed Sheets or Docs Add an editable Office surface to your application or agent product, and connect your data through Facade APIs. Quick start
Process content without an editor Reuse content plugins, models, commands, and calculation in Node.js for editing, snapshots, and automated tasks. Headless guide
Develop custom features or editors Reuse the engines, UI components, plugin boundaries, dependency injection, and command/undo systems. Follow existing features to extend Sheets and Docs or develop your own editors. Open-source architecture
**Coordinate edits and undo/redo across features.** Inserting a row inside a filter range changes both the base content and the filter range; undo needs to restore both. Each feature supplies its own changes and undo data, and the command composes their execution and history. The architecture walkthrough explains how to extend these editing workflows. ### Quick start: an open-source spreadsheet editor In a browser application using a bundler such as Vite: ```bash pnpm add @univerjs/presets @univerjs/preset-sheets-core ``` Create the container before initializing Univer: ```html
``` ```ts import { UniverSheetsCorePreset } from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core' import UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/locales/en-US' import { createUniver, LocaleType, mergeLocales } from '@univerjs/presets' import '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/lib/index.css' const { univerAPI } = createUniver({ locale: LocaleType.EN_US, locales: { [LocaleType.EN_US]: mergeLocales(UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS), }, presets: [ UniverSheetsCorePreset({ container: 'app', }), ], }) univerAPI.createWorkbook({}) ``` Your page now contains a spreadsheet editor. Use the returned `univerAPI` to work with its content. This example uses open-source packages and needs no commercial Univer license or Server SDK. For component frameworks, retain the `univer` instance returned by `createUniver` and call `univer.dispose()` when the component unmounts. See the [lifecycle guide](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/getting-started/lifecycle). Presets compose plugins and register their Facade APIs. For manual control, see the [Plugin Mode example](#manual-plugin-composition) below. The [installation guide](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/getting-started/installation) covers both modes, peer dependencies, and framework integrations. Keep coordinated `@univerjs/*` packages on the same version. Commercial packages must use the matching release line; independently released packages such as icons follow their declared compatibility. See the [API Stability Policy](./docs/API_STABILITY.md). ### Connect your application to editable content Facade APIs are the application-facing interface to workbooks, worksheets, and ranges. Continue from the quick start to populate a quotation, update a quantity from application code, and read the recalculated total: ```ts // Wait for formula controllers before editing a newly created workbook. await new Promise((resolve) => { if (univerAPI.getCurrentLifecycleStage() >= univerAPI.Enum.LifecycleStages.Steady) { resolve() return } const listener = univerAPI.addEvent(univerAPI.Event.LifeCycleChanged, ({ stage }) => { if (stage === univerAPI.Enum.LifecycleStages.Steady) { listener.dispose() resolve() } }) }) const workbook = univerAPI.getActiveWorkbook()! const sheet = workbook.getActiveSheet() sheet.getRange('A1:D4').setValues([ ['Item', 'Quantity', 'Unit price', 'Amount'], ['Seats', 2, 25, '=B2*C2'], ['Support', 1, 100, '=B3*C3'], ['Total', '', '', '=SUM(D2:D3)'], ]) // An application control or agent can make the same edit. sheet.getRange('B2').setValue(4) univerAPI.getFormula().onCalculationResultApplied().then(() => { console.log(sheet.getRange('D4').getValue()) // 200 localStorage.setItem('quotation', JSON.stringify(workbook.save())) }).catch(console.error) ``` The editor and your application operate on the same workbook; formula changes are recalculated automatically. `workbook.save()` returns a JSON snapshot containing the workbook and its registered plugin data. Your application owns persistence; this example uses browser storage. On a later page load, after initialization, restore the snapshot **instead of creating a blank workbook**: ```ts const saved = localStorage.getItem('quotation') if (saved) { univerAPI.createWorkbook(JSON.parse(saved)) } ``` This workflow uses only open-source packages. Snapshot persistence is separate from XLSX import and export, which uses the separately distributed file-conversion capabilities. Use public Facade APIs for application integration; the source links below explain internal implementation and extension points. See the [API Stability Policy](./docs/API_STABILITY.md) before depending on an extension point.
Advanced: compose plugins manually (Plugin Mode) Use Plugin Mode when you need precise control over plugin selection, dependencies, or loading. The preset above handles this composition for you. This alternative initialization uses the same `app` container and the Sheets Core preset's browser plugin stack without a Worker. Use it **instead of** the preset initialization, then run the same quotation example with the returned `univerAPI`. ```bash pnpm add @univerjs/core @univerjs/design @univerjs/docs @univerjs/docs-ui \ @univerjs/engine-formula @univerjs/engine-render @univerjs/network \ @univerjs/sheets @univerjs/sheets-ui @univerjs/sheets-formula \ @univerjs/sheets-formula-ui @univerjs/sheets-numfmt \ @univerjs/sheets-numfmt-ui @univerjs/ui ``` ```ts import { LocaleType, mergeLocales, Univer } from '@univerjs/core' import { FUniver } from '@univerjs/core/facade' import DesignEnUS from { UniverFormulaEnginePlugin } from '@univerjs/engine-formula' import FormulaEnUS from '@univerjs/engine-formula/locale/en-US' import { UniverRenderEnginePlugin } from '@univerjs/engine-render' import UniverUIPlugin } from '@univerjs/ui' import UIEnUS from '@univerjs/ui/locale/en-US' import '@univerjs/design/lib/index.css' import '@univerjs/ui/lib/index.css' import '@univerjs/docs-ui/lib/index.css' import '@univerjs/sheets-ui/lib/index.css' import '@univerjs/sheets-formula-ui/lib/index.css' import '@univerjs/sheets-numfmt-ui/lib/index.css' import '@univerjs/network/facade' import [LocaleType.EN_US]: mergeLocales( DesignEnUS, DocsUIEnUS, FormulaEnUS, SheetsEnUS, SheetsFormulaEnUS, SheetsFormulaUIEnUS, SheetsNumfmtUIEnUS, SheetsUIEnUS, UIEnUS, ), }, }) univer.registerPlugin(UniverNetworkPlugin) univer.registerPlugin(UniverDocsPlugin) univer.registerPlugin(UniverRenderEnginePlugin) univer.registerPlugin(UniverUIPlugin, { container: 'app' }) univer.registerPlugin(UniverSheetsFormulaPlugin) univer.registerPlugin(UniverSheetsFormulaUIPlugin) const univerAPI = FUniver.newAPI(univer) univerAPI.createWorkbook({}) ``` The Docs plugins support spreadsheet rich-text editing. When adding a feature, include its corresponding Facade extensions, locale bundles, and UI styles. Dispose `univer` when its container is unmounted.

## 🏗️ Explore the open-source architecture

### Give custom features clear boundaries Univer organizes content logic and UI interaction in separate plugins. Feature plugins manage rules and content changes; UI plugins provide the interface and user interactions. For example, `sheets-filter` manages filter ranges and rules, while `sheets-filter-ui` provides panels, menus, and shortcuts. ```mermaid %%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%% %% A layered overview, not a complete dependency graph. %% Group arrows indicate reuse of the layer below; internal arrows show selected dependencies. flowchart TD subgraph FEATURES["Feature Plugins"] direction LR FUI["Filter
UI Plugin"] VUI["Data Validation
UI Plugin"] FILTER["Filter Plugin"] VALIDATION["Data Validation Plugin"] FUI --> FILTER VUI --> VALIDATION end subgraph PRODUCTS["Product Plugins"] direction LR SUI["Sheets UI Plugin"] SHEETS["Sheets Plugin"] SUI --> SHEETS end subgraph FOUNDATION["Core Framework & Plugins"] direction LR UI["UI Plugin"] FORMULA["Formula Engine Plugin"] RENDER["Render Engine Plugin"] CORE["Core"] UI --> RENDER RENDER --> CORE FORMULA --> CORE end FEATURES --> PRODUCTS PRODUCTS --> FOUNDATION classDef logic fill:#eff6ff,color:#17365f,stroke:#93b4df,stroke-width:1.5px classDef ui fill:#f0fdf4,color:#17543a,stroke:#91c8a7,stroke-width:1.5px classDef shared fill:#f6f7f9,color:#334155,stroke:#bac3ce,stroke-width:1.5px classDef feature fill:#172d50,color:#ffffff,stroke:#172d50 class FUI,VUI ui class FILTER,VALIDATION logic class SUI,SHEETS logic class UI,FORMULA,RENDER,CORE shared style FEATURES fill:#f7fcf9,stroke:#b5d8c1,color:#17543a style PRODUCTS fill:#f5f9ff,stroke:#b6cbea,color:#17365f style FOUNDATION fill:#fafbfc,stroke:#cbd2dc,color:#334155 ``` **Figure 1: three plugin layers.** Feature plugins build on product plugins, which reuse the core framework and plugins. Group arrows show dependencies on the layer below; Core provides content models, commands, dependency injection, and lifecycle management. Some plugins and dependencies are omitted. New features keep their rules in their own plugins and cooperate through public services, commands, and defined extension points. UI plugins build on shared UI services and components. Dependencies are explicit at two levels: - **Between plugins:** `DependentOn` declares runtime plugin dependencies. The plugin service orders them, and lifecycle stages separate dependency registration, content initialization, and UI initialization. - **Inside plugins:** dependency injection connects controllers and services through declared dependencies. Supported overrides let an application replace an implementation, adapt a platform service, or supply a test double. Instance-scoped injectors keep application state separate between Univer instances. Disposable registration also gives commands, listeners, components, and icons a cleanup path when their owner is disposed. The [filter plugin](./packages/sheets-filter/src/plugin.ts) and its [UI plugin](./packages/sheets-filter-ui/src/plugin.ts) show these boundaries in working code.
Inside a feature: Model, Controller, Service, and the UI foundation For filtering, `sheets-filter` owns content logic and `sheets-filter-ui` owns UI interaction. Each module has a focused responsibility. ```mermaid %%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%% %% Every arrow means contains. This is code organization, not execution order. flowchart LR FEATURE["Filter Feature"] LOGIC["Filter Plugin"] UI["Filter UI Plugin"] MODEL["Model"] SERVICE["Service"] CONTROLLER["Controller"] COMMAND["Command / Mutation"] FACADE["Facade API"] VIEW["View"] UICTRL["UI Controller"] UISERVICE["UI Service"] FEATURE --> LOGIC FEATURE --> UI LOGIC --> MODEL LOGIC --> SERVICE LOGIC --> CONTROLLER LOGIC --> COMMAND LOGIC --> FACADE UI --> VIEW UI --> UICTRL UI --> UISERVICE classDef logic fill:#eff6ff,color:#17365f,stroke:#93b4df,stroke-width:1.5px classDef ui fill:#f0fdf4,color:#17543a,stroke:#91c8a7,stroke-width:1.5px classDef shared fill:#f6f7f9,color:#334155,stroke:#bac3ce,stroke-width:1.5px classDef feature fill:#172d50,color:#ffffff,stroke:#172d50 class FEATURE feature class LOGIC,MODEL,SERVICE,CONTROLLER,COMMAND,FACADE logic class UI,VIEW,UICTRL,UISERVICE ui ``` **Figure 2: code organization. Arrows mean “contains.”** Both plugins can contain Controllers and Services: logic Controllers coordinate content changes and related features; UI Controllers connect menus, shortcuts, and interactions, with UI Services managing panel state. These responsibilities give new features a consistent structure to implement and test. The UI foundation follows the same division. **`@univerjs/design`** supplies shared components and styles, **`@univerjs/ui`** provides workbench services such as menus, shortcuts, panels, and component registration, and **`@univerjs/icons`** supplies icons. A feature registers its components and icons, contributes menus, and attaches its rendering through these extension points. Teams can add a panel or toolbar feature while reusing the application's UI infrastructure. See the [UI overview](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/ui/overview) and the filter plugin's [component and icon registration](./packages/sheets-filter-ui/src/controllers/components.controller.ts).
### Compose cross-feature edits and undo/redo For example, when rows are inserted inside a filter range, the filter plugin supplies the corresponding range change and its undo data. The row command composes the base edit and participating feature changes, executes them, and records their undo/redo information together. The row insertion feature can use the shared extension mechanism while the filter plugin owns its range-update rules. The command system distinguishes three kinds of action: - **Command** orchestrates a business action and the changes it requires. - **Mutation** changes content saved in a snapshot, with serializable parameters. - **Operation** changes transient state, such as an open panel or the scroll position. **A shared structure for undo/redo.** For an undoable edit, the feature implementation supplies the forward mutations and corresponding inverse mutations, and the Command records them through `IUndoRedoService`. When one action affects several features, the Command can combine their changes and undo data in a single undo/redo record, so the user can undo and redo the complete action. See [extending commands](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/custom-command). Features still need to cooperate. **Interceptors and reference-range handlers give that cooperation a defined place.** At supported extension points, plugins contribute checks or related mutations; interceptor priorities control ordering where the API defines it.
Example: commands, callbacks, feature coordination, and undo/redo ```mermaid %%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%% %% Simplified insert-row example. A command composes mutations and records undo after success. %% Events may also fire for nested command executions; not every callback is drawn. flowchart TD BEFORE["Before execution
Inspect or cancel"] CMD["Insert-row Command"] BASE["Row mutations"] EXT["Feature extension points
Filter range changes"] MODEL["Execute combined mutations"] UNDO["Record undo and redo"] AFTER["After execution
Notify listeners"] BEFORE --> CMD CMD --> BASE CMD --> EXT BASE --> MODEL EXT --> MODEL MODEL --> UNDO UNDO --> AFTER classDef entry fill:#f6f7f9,color:#334155,stroke:#bac3ce,stroke-width:1.5px classDef core fill:#eff6ff,color:#17365f,stroke:#93b4df,stroke-width:1.5px classDef extension fill:#f0fdf4,color:#17543a,stroke:#91c8a7,stroke-width:1.5px class BEFORE,AFTER entry class CMD,BASE,MODEL,UNDO core class EXT extension ``` This diagram simplifies an insert-row workflow. Nested command executions have their own callbacks; it does not show every event or the separate Operation path. See the [row command](./packages/sheets/src/commands/commands/insert-row-col.command.ts), [filter controller](./packages/sheets-filter/src/controllers/sheets-filter.controller.ts), and [interceptor service](./packages/sheets/src/services/sheet-interceptor/sheet-interceptor.service.ts).
These boundaries support a practical testing strategy: test models and services independently, replace external dependencies through DI, and add regression cases for combined actions and undo/redo. The [filter controller tests](./packages/sheets-filter/src/controllers/__tests__/sheets-filter.controller.spec.ts) exercise row and column changes and their effect on filtering. ### Connect applications and agents through Facade APIs and events The repository includes the content models, formula engine, and Canvas rendering and layout engine behind the editors. They are shared building blocks: spreadsheet rich text, for example, reuses document layout and rendering. Custom features can build on these engines instead of implementing a separate content stack. Read about the [formula engine architecture](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/formula) and [rendering engine architecture](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/rendering). Browser editors, Node.js Headless tasks, and appropriately composed Workers can reuse the corresponding content plugins, models, commands, and calculation. See [Headless Univer](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/getting-started/node) and the [isomorphic architecture](./docs/ISOMORPHIC.md). `ICommandService` exposes execution callbacks so plugins can observe commands before and after execution. Facade APIs wrap the underlying capabilities in application objects such as `FWorkbook`, `FWorksheet`, and `FRange`. Each plugin contributes its own Facade extensions, **typed events through `univerAPI.Event`**, and **enums through `univerAPI.Enum`**. Application code can discover event names and constants from one entry point instead of importing private services or repeating strings. For example, `BeforeCommandExecute` can inspect and cancel an execution; `CommandExecuted` reports executions to listeners. Listeners return disposables, and cancellation applies where the event supports it. Facade extensions stay with their feature packages, so a content API does not have to pull in unrelated UI APIs. See the [Facade design](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/facade), [command callbacks and event bridge](./packages/core/src/facade/f-univer.ts), and [Enum entry point](./packages/core/src/facade/f-enum.ts). The repository provides working feature implementations and patterns for extending them. Read the [filter implementation walkthrough](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/anatomy) for a complete example, or the [API Stability Policy](./docs/API_STABILITY.md) before depending on an extension point.

## 🧩 Extend your application with Univer Office SDK

When you want more ready-to-integrate capabilities, compose the corresponding **Univer Office SDK** modules: additional content types, advanced editing plugins, collaboration, file conversion, and agent tooling. They extend the same content models, plugin architecture, command system, and Facade design introduced above, so you can build on your existing integration.
Part How it extends the foundation
Open-source Web SDK core · this repository Open-source models, engines, plugins, UI foundation, and Sheets and Docs capabilities, with corresponding Headless content operations. Use them in commercial applications under Apache-2.0.

Server SDK Extends the same content models and mutation conventions with real-time collaboration, revision history, and Office file conversion. Integrates with your application's identity, permissions, and storage.
AI SDK extensions Reuse Web SDK Headless and Facade capabilities to provide composable Node.js APIs and CLI building blocks for agents to inspect, edit, and check content, with collaboration and Worktree review integrations.

See the [feature comparison](https://univer.ai/compare/), including its **Open source only** filter, for detailed coverage and [plans and licensing](https://univer.ai/pricing/) for commercial options.
How shared content models connect editing, collaboration, and files These capabilities operate on serializable **Unit snapshots**, including Sheets' `IWorkbookData`, Docs' `IDocumentData`, Slides' `ISlideData`, and canvases' `IBoardData` (called **Boards** in the API). These types come from core and the respective product packages; current Slides and Boards capabilities are separately distributed commercial products. The shared Unit conventions let browser editors, backend services, and agents work with the same content. Commands orchestrate edits; **Mutations describe content changes**. Collaboration packages those mutations into **changesets**, applies **operational transformation (OT)** to concurrent changes, and manages confirmed revisions and snapshots. History can reconstruct a revision from a snapshot and subsequent changesets. Read the [collaboration design](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/ot) and [Collaboration SDK overview](https://docs.univer.ai/server/collaboration/overview). **Exchange** maps Office file structures to and from Univer content snapshots. For OOXML formats such as **XLSX, DOCX, and PPTX**, it parses the file into the corresponding Sheet, Doc, or Slide data and generates the file representation on export. The converted content can enter the same editing, calculation, collaboration, and agent workflows. See [Office file import and export](https://docs.univer.ai/server/import-export/node).
How AI SDK gives agents the same content capabilities AI SDK builds on the Web SDK's **Headless content models, commands, calculation, and Facade APIs**. It exposes structured TypeScript APIs and optional Commander presets that applications can compose into their own Office CLI or agent tools. - **Understand, discover, and edit.** Inspection returns structured content. API Reference helps the agent find Facade symbols and signatures shipped with its SDK. Facade execution distinguishes read and write modes, captures mutations, and works with explicit synchronization and commit results. See [content operations](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/content-operations). - **Check the rendered result.** A browser Render Runtime reuses Web SDK rendering for screenshots. Slide layout lint adds structured findings for issues such as off-page or overlapping text, giving the agent evidence for another editing pass. See [visual inspection](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/visual-inspection). - **Edit drafts for human review.** With the corresponding collaboration and Web capabilities, agents can edit and verify an isolated Worktree draft over several rounds, then hand it to a person to review, merge, or reopen. The workflow uses the same snapshots, mutations, and revision conventions. See [Worktree](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/worktree). For repeated calls, optional [Worker pools and a daemon](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/runtime-architecture) reuse loaded content instances and reduce repeated initialization. Your application owns the root CLI, targets, authorization, and output. Explore the [AI SDK package catalog](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/packages) to select the required capabilities.

## ✨ Why OpenMotion ### 1. A full-stack agentic video studio **Code video with HTML.** OpenMotion uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript to describe scenes, typography, layout, transitions and timing. Recorded footage, generated clips, images, music and voice-over become media inside the composition. The same project opens in Studio and renders to MP4. ![Your local agent, optional media-model accounts and creative resources feed a workflow of understanding the reference, coding scenes, generating missing media, editing and rendering MP4 with reusable source.](docs/readme/diagrams/creation-stack.svg) **Write it. Watch it. Change it. Render it.** Ask your agent to replace the product, tighten the hook, add a presenter, change the captions or try another ending. It edits the project source; you review the result in the visual editor. Local MCP clients use the project tools, while agents with shell access can follow the Skills and pinned CLI workflow. [Agent setup](#agent-setup) · [Native composition guide](skills/openmotion-production/references/native.md) · [Example HTML project](template-library/product-promo/index.html) If historical media are unavailable, an Agent restore is refused before changing the project. The editor shows a dismissible error with the affected file paths and confirms that the current project is unchanged. Review your video, arrange clips and export from the same Studio workspace. #### What you can change in Studio | In the Studio | What you can do today | | --- | --- | | **Story and timeline** | Import and arrange media; have the agent trim, reorder and revise against a script or confirmed timecodes | | **Motion and captions** | Author animated type, transitions, callouts, charts and captions around your content | | **Media and sound** | Import your material and generate images, video, music and TTS voice-over through the built-in model integrations | | **Image revision** | Generate candidates with a reference-capable image model and adopt a replacement while preserving timing and animation | | **Preview and versions** | Review in Studio, edit by hand or with your agent, and return to the project for the next revision | | **Export and source** | Render a fixed version to MP4 and retain the HTML, CSS, JavaScript and media | > “Keep the reveal we approved. Replace the middle scene with this screen recording, tighten the opening using these timecodes, and hold our final CTA for two more seconds.” [Projects and versions](docs/project-workspace.md) #### From a reference clip to an editable remake 1. **Break down the reference.** Pick a sequence. Record its shot order, transitions and sound cues in Motion.md, and mark what you want to replace. 2. **Rebuild the shots.** Your agent rebuilds the HTML scenes using your brand kit, copy and visuals, then arranges them on an editable timeline in Studio. 3. **Compare the cuts.** Watch the same moment in the original and the remake. Adjust the timing, movement and sound, then play the sequence through. 4. **Export and share.** Render the MP4 and keep the HTML source and media. To share a project others can adapt, include its Motion.md, a preview and assets you can redistribute. [Project contribution checklist](library/ENTRY_TEMPLATE.md) ### 2. Free and open source. Use your local agent and bring your own keys. **Choose your agent.** WorkBuddy, Codex, Claude Code and DeepSeek Harness have installation instructions. Other buttons open the shared MCP and CLI setup.

| Bring your own… | Make it work for your video | | --- | --- | | **🤖 Agent — BYOA** | Connect your existing local agent through Skills and MCP, with CLI access where supported. Keep your preferred client, account and working context. | | **🔑 Keys — BYOK** | Connect supported media-provider API keys in Model Settings. Choose models for images, video, music and TTS; supported local media integrations can use your existing agent login. | | **🎨 Brand and material** | Add your logo, fonts, screenshots, camera footage, script and music. Keep identity and approved assets in the Brand Kit section of Motion.md. | | **🧩 Starting resources** | Browse references, motion components, templates and community Skills. Pick a direction, give the source or reference to your agent, and make it yours. | **The OpenMotion creation pipeline is open source: Skills, project tools, model integrations, Studio and rendering.** Run it locally, inspect the implementation and extend the parts you need. OpenMotion charges no software subscription or per-render fee for this local workflow. You can also work with your own footage, images and audio without invoking media-generation APIs. Provider credentials stay in your workspace, separate from the video project. Your agent and media providers bill any subscriptions or usage to your own accounts. [Agent setup and compatibility](docs/agent-adapters.md) ### 3. 300+ Motion.md guides for video recreation OpenMotion introduces **Motion.md**: a Markdown format for shot order, timing, transitions and the assets you can replace. The online library brings reference videos and their motion guides into the same detail page. The Brand Kit section records your identity, voice and approved product facts; the Design section can reference an independent `DESIGN.md` for visual rules. Keep the reference’s motion and pacing while making the result recognizably yours. To share an industry or brand system, use the [Motion Package v0.2 draft](docs/motion-package-spec.md) and [authoring toolkit](packages/motion-package/README.md). The included recipe demonstrates two content presets; automatic Studio import and rendered fidelity remain separate from package validation. ![Motion.md and brand context](docs/readme/diagrams/creative-context.svg) #### Find a template, then make it yours Browse by **reference brand, use case and video type**, or search for a specific idea. Preview candidates and adopt the results into the same project your agent and Studio edit. The supported local image path can reuse your existing agent login. Connect fal.ai in **Model Settings** and refresh its catalog to find GPT Image 2.6, Nano Banana 2.1, FLUX.3, Seedance 2.5, Kling 4.0, Wan 3.0 and Eleven v4. Browse and preview first; choose **Open and edit** to create an independent editable copy. Setup provides a direct library link even before the chat reloads MCP. See the [installation reply rules](docs/install-onboarding.md#installation-success-reply). During video creation and editing, the chat stays free of preview areas. OpenMotion presents the editable Studio when the final video is ready to preview, then shows [one final-video preview](docs/inline-video.md) after MP4 export and verification. Host-native playback takes priority; Codex embeds the video in the final reply. The optional MCP App player is used only when the host cannot preview the video, never alongside another preview of the same export. Native-host acceptance of an installed build remains separate. If MCP tools are missing or fail to connect, use the installed [connection diagnosis and recovery guide](docs/npm-installation.md#missing-mcp-tools-or-a-failed-connection) to inspect the actual host configuration and verify the original workspace before continuing. Use Git, npm and **Node.js 26.11.1**. Source-based preview and export also need Chrome/Chromium and FFmpeg/FFprobe. [Runtime setup](docs/usage.md) ```sh git -c filter.lfs.process= -c filter.lfs.smudge= -c filter.lfs.required=false clone --depth 1 --single-branch --branch main https://github.com/nexu-io/openmotion.git cd openmotion npm ci npm run build:studio npm start ``` Full reference videos and optional template archives download through Git LFS only when requested. The local Studio and MCP use the same files; `openmotion_list_templates` returns a searchable local index, and `openmotion_get_template` returns local guide content and absolute source paths. Imported large images and videos retain existing CMS links; new contribution media can use Git LFS. Local edits appear on the next catalog read. The plugin root is this checkout: `.codex-plugin/plugin.json` loads its `skills/` and `.mcp.json`, which launches the root `mcp.ts`. Start stdio with `npm run mcp` or use an absolute path in [manual MCP configuration](#manual-mcp). [Local template workflow](docs/template-repository.md#run-from-a-local-clone). #### Bring it into your agent For Codex with plugin support, run from the checkout: ```sh bash scripts/install-motion.command ``` **WorkBuddy** · Import the OpenMotion connector in WorkBuddy or add its `mcp.json` as a custom MCP server. items.readme_text:
Craft Anything

English · 日本語 · 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · 한국어 · Español · Français · Tiếng Việt · Português · ไทย · Türkçe

See how any website, app or game works, then have AI build your own version; an open-source, clean-room engine in pure Rust.
Point it at a target, say what you want, and it studies the original with real inspection tools,
has a coding agent build a new project, checks the result against the original and refines it.


Download Craft Anything · ArtCraft · All Crafting Apps



A website project: each check says how alike the build is, you approve anything outside the rules, and the plan shows what's left.

> [!NOTE] > **ArtCraft is a community of artists from all walks of life.** Painters, photographers, > filmmakers, illustrators, designers, animators, hobbyists, and people who picked up a pencil > last week. If you make things, you're one of us. **[Come say hi on Discord](https://discord.gg/artcraft).**

How it works · Two ways to use it · AI · Agents · Under the hood · Get started · Status · Downloads · Discord


🔍 Study anything

Websites, desktop apps, phone apps, games and files: real inspection tools find out how they're built and what they do, with the evidence behind every answer.

🛠️ Build your own

Say what you want ("Recreate this website", "Recreate this game's gameplay in Rust") and a coding agent builds a new project in the stack you ask for.

✅ Checked, not guessed

Every build is compared with the original (pages at three screen widths, a game's own self-test, an app's runs) and refined until it's close.

🤖 Agent-ready

320 tools, each one a CLI command and an MCP tool, so any agent can drive the same engine the app uses. No AI is needed to inspect.

## How it works Point Craft Anything at a target, say what you want, and press Start. It works in four steps, asking you in plain words when a decision is yours: 1. **Study:** inspect the original: its pages at every width, its code, its files, how it runs. 2. **Build:** a coding agent builds a new project, in the language, framework or engine your request names (or a sensible default). 3. **Check:** compare the build with the original and list what doesn't match yet. 4. **Ready:** open, play or preview the result, or ask for changes and it refines it.

Make: pick what to recreate, say what you want, press Start.
Ready: play the game, or ask for changes below.
## Two ways to use it - **Simple** (default): "What do you want to make?" Pick a website, app or game, describe it, press Start. A project page shows the four steps (Study → Build → Check → Ready), what the agent is doing in plain words, question and approval cards, how alike the result is, and buttons to open the result or its folder. Ask for changes in the box at the bottom. "Just look inside" opens a target for questions without building anything (in Deep mode). - **Advanced**: the full workbench: every tool (Ctrl/Cmd+K), functions, strings, pseudo-C, disassembly, hex, call graphs, evidence, unknowns, jobs, logs and the agent console. Both modes drive the same engine. ## Clean room or Deep - **Clean room** (the default): nothing inside the original is read, not its code, files or page source. Craft Anything works from what you can see: pictures you add, the website as a visitor sees it (screenshots, visible text, measured layout, colours, fonts and spacing, menus opened) and, when you allow it, a picture of the app's window. Tools that would look inside are refused and say how to turn on Deep mode. - **Deep**: every tool is used, for your private use. A program's code and files are read with the built-in engines (and Ghidra when it's installed), a website's JavaScript is read and its start page watched, and the builder may use all of them. Clean room is a rule about what Craft Anything offers and refuses. It is not an operating-system sandbox: it doesn't isolate your computer. A coding agent you run still acts as you, and what it can read, write or run depends on its own permissions. Which of an agent's own tools Craft Anything can refuse differs by agent; for Claude Code's tools in chats and questions, see [`docs/claude-code.md`](docs/claude-code.md). Switch in the title bar or Settings, with `settings_set deep_mode true`, or for one CLI run with `--deep` (or `--clean-room`).


Advanced: functions, pseudo-C, the agent and the evidence behind every answer.

## AI Building needs a coding agent on your computer. **Claude Code** is supported first: Craft Anything runs your own, unmodified `claude` program, which uses your own sign-in; Craft Anything never sees or handles your account. Your use of it falls under your own agreement with Anthropic. See [docs/claude-code.md](docs/claude-code.md) for how and why. A Codex adapter exists but hasn't been verified on a real install yet. **GitHub Copilot** can use your installed Copilot CLI through ACP: sign in separately with `copilot login`. **Grok Build** can use your installed `grok` program through ACP (`grok agent stdio`): sign in separately with `grok login`. See [docs/grok.md](docs/grok.md). Other agents that speak ACP (Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, opencode, goose, Hermes, Maki, Devin) can be switched to it per backend; of those, Maki and Devin have been run live (Devin authenticates with the backend's stored key — its own CLI sign-in doesn't count over ACP). Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, xAI (Grok, when `XAI_API_KEY` is set) and local OpenAI-compatible servers are available for questions and analysis (Settings → AI). ## Built for agents Every tool is also a CLI subcommand and an MCP tool, so an agent can study a target or run a whole rebuild without the app: ```sh craft-anything-cli commands # every tool, by toolset craft-anything-cli mcp # serve them to any MCP client craft-anything-cli rebuild https://example.com "Recreate this website" ``` Results are evidence records with their confidence, coverage and limitations; big ones come back as a summary first and are paged with `core_evidence_browse`. `craft-anything-cli setup` connects Craft Anything to coding-agent apps. ## Under the hood A pure-Rust reverse-engineering engine with 320 tools (300 in the engine, the rest from the AI and setup layers) for native programs, .NET, Java, Android, Apple, Electron/JavaScript, websites, firmware, packet captures, databases and game files. Its own decoders, disassembler and decompiler work without any outside program; Deep mode uses them all, and Ghidra when it's installed. It powers the desktop app (egui), the CLI and the MCP server, and parts of it run in the browser as WebAssembly. The full list is in [docs/tools.md](docs/tools.md). ## Get started Requires Rust **1.97 or newer** (a dependency needs it; `rustup update`). On Debian or Ubuntu, the desktop app also needs: ```sh sudo apt-get install build-essential libxkbcommon-dev libxkbcommon-x11-0 libwayland-dev libx11-dev libxrandr-dev libxi-dev libgl1-mesa-dev libgtk-3-dev ``` Then: ```sh git clone https://github.com/storytold/craft-anything && cd craft-anything cargo run --release -p craft-anything # the desktop app cargo install --path apps/craft-anything-cli # the CLI, as `craft-anything-cli` craft-anything-cli doctor # checks the install, coding agents and engines ``` Building needs a coding agent signed in on your computer (see [AI](#ai)); `doctor` says what's missing. Rebuild from the command line (questions are asked in the terminal): ```sh craft-anything-cli rebuild https://example.com "Recreate this website" craft-anything-cli rebuild - "A snake game in Rust" --rounds 1 craft-anything-cli rebuild https://example.com "Make the header blue" --continue-in "" craft-anything-cli rebuild - "Add a contact form" --project-folder "" --existing edit ``` New projects go in `Documents/Craft Anything` (change it in Settings → General). Each project folder holds `craft.json` (the request, target, status and history), `capture/` (what was recorded from the target), `app/` (the generated project), `checks/` (each comparison against the original), `investigation.cany/` (evidence) and `inbox/` (open questions). A project can also start in a folder you pick (Choose a folder… under Start, or `--project-folder`). If it already has files, you say what they are: the app itself, which the builder edits in place, or material to start from, with the app built in `app/` beside them (Settings → General can remember the answer). Settings → General also lists projects from more folders; removing one only takes it off the list. ## Status > [!IMPORTANT] > **Status:** Craft Anything is in early alpha. What works today, what is partial and what's next: > > - **Works today:** the desktop app (Simple and Advanced), the CLI and the MCP server; the > Study → Build → Check → Ready workflow for websites, apps and games with Claude Code as the > builder; website checks at three screen widths; game rebuilds in Unity, Unreal or Godot; Deep > mode with Ghidra; generated pictures and 3D models (opt-in, your own fal.ai key); plugins (MCP > servers, and WASM components in builds with the `wasm-plugins` option). > - **Partly there:** building with API keys and other coding agents (built, not yet run live), > behaviour checks for apps and games, a few engine tools tested only against stand-ins. > - **Released:** public releases with installers for Windows, macOS, Linux and FreeBSD are > published on the [Releases page](https://github.com/storytold/craft-anything/releases); they are > still alpha. > - **Next:** the managed tier. > > [docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md) has the detail and how each part was checked, > [docs/tool-status.md](docs/tool-status.md) the tool-by-tool checklist, and > [docs/ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md) the plan, item by item. Please file issues, or tell us what > broke on [Discord](https://discord.gg/artcraft). **Responsible use.** Use Craft Anything on software you own or are allowed to examine. It never bypasses DRM, logins or anti-cheat. Rebuilds recreate layout, style and behaviour from evidence; the agent is told not to copy logos, photos or text unless you confirm you own them or have permission. **Installing dependencies runs code.** When a builder installs a project's dependencies, the commands run on your computer, and the packages can run code while they install. npm runs each package's install scripts by default, and Rust build scripts and Python source packages run their own setup code. Craft Anything asks before a command of a kind it hasn't seen in this project (`npm`, `cargo`…). Choosing "always allow" for `npm` lets every later npm command run without asking, so only do that for a project whose dependencies you trust. To install npm packages without their install scripts, run `npm install --ignore-scripts`. ## Downloads On GitHub, the [latest release](https://github.com/storytold/craft-anything/releases/latest) has every build listed below, and [all releases](https://github.com/storytold/craft-anything/releases) has earlier versions and their notes. `` in the file names is the version number, and `SHA256SUMS.txt` lists a checksum for every file. ### Windows | Build | Installer | Portable | |---|---|---| | x64 (64-bit Intel/AMD) | `craft-anything--windows-x64.msi` | `craft-anything--windows-x64-portable.zip` | | arm64 (Snapdragon and other ARM PCs) | `craft-anything--windows-arm64.msi` | `craft-anything--windows-arm64-portable.zip` | | x86 (32-bit) | `craft-anything--windows-x86.msi` | `craft-anything--windows-x86-portable.zip` | Installers and executables are code-signed. The portable zip keeps its settings next to the app. ### macOS | Build | File | Notes | |---|---|---| | App, universal (Apple silicon + Intel) | `craft-anything--macos-universal.dmg` | Signed and notarized | | Command-line tool, universal | `craft-anything-cli--macos-universal.zip` | Signed and notarized; see below if macOS blocks it | Versions after 0.2.0 include the command-line tool in the app, so builds don't need the separate zip. You only need it to use the command line without the app. A browser download of the zip can stop with "Apple could not verify craft-anything-cli" (a lone program can't carry its notarization with it, so macOS has to look it up online). A download from the terminal isn't checked this way, so use this instead: ```sh ver=0.2.0 # change this to the version you want curl -fLO "https://github.com/storytold/craft-anything/releases/download/v$ver/craft-anything-cli-$ver-macos-universal.zip" ditto -x -k "craft-anything-cli-$ver-macos-universal.zip" . mkdir -p ~/.local/bin mv "craft-anything-cli-$ver-macos-universal/craft-anything-cli" ~/.local/bin/ ~/.local/bin/craft-anything-cli --version ``` To run it as just `craft-anything-cli`, add `~/.local/bin` to your `PATH`. If you already have the blocked copy, press Done (not Move to Bin), then run `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine `, or allow it in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway. #### Checking that a Mac download is signed and notarized Each Mac release is signed with a Developer ID certificate and notarized by Apple. To check a download yourself, run these in Terminal (replace `` with the version and the paths with yours): ```sh # The disk image: "accepted" and "source=Notarized Developer ID" mean it passed spctl --assess --type open --context context:primary-signature -v "craft-anything--macos-universal.dmg" # The notarization ticket is attached: prints "The validate action worked!" xcrun stapler validate "craft-anything--macos-universal.dmg" # The app, after you open the disk image: the signature must verify codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=2 "/Volumes//Craft Anything.app" spctl --assess --type execute --verbose "/Volumes//Craft Anything.app" # The command-line tool: a bare program can't carry a ticket, so macOS checks it online codesign --verify --strict --verbose=2 ~/.local/bin/craft-anything-cli codesign -dv --verbose=4 ~/.local/bin/craft-anything-cli 2>&1 | grep Authority ``` The `Authority` lines should name a "Developer ID Application" certificate. If a check fails, don't run the file; report it with the output and the release tag. ### Linux | Format | x86_64 | aarch64 (ARM64) | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | AppImage | `craft-anything--linux-x86_64.AppImage` | `craft-anything--linux-aarch64.AppImage` | Runs anywhere; updates itself with [AppImageUpdate](https://github.com/AppImageCommunity/AppImageUpdate) (`.zsync` files) | | Flatpak | `craft-anything--linux-x86_64.flatpak` | `craft-anything--linux-aarch64.flatpak` | Sandboxed, so it can't start a browser on your computer, which studying websites needs (use another package for that); `flatpak install --user ` | | Debian/Ubuntu | `craft-anything--linux-x86_64.deb` | `craft-anything--linux-aarch64.deb` | | | Fedora/RHEL/openSUSE | `craft-anything--linux-x86_64.rpm` | `craft-anything--linux-aarch64.rpm` | | | Tarball | `craft-anything--linux-x86_64.tar.gz` | `craft-anything--linux-aarch64.tar.gz` | Unpack anywhere | RISC-V (riscv64): `craft-anything--linux-riscv64.tar.gz`, a tarball only. The AppImage carries the CLI too: run ` --cli ` (for example ` --cli mcp` for an MCP client), or make a link to the AppImage named `craft-anything-cli` and run that. ### FreeBSD | Build | File | |---|---| | x86_64 | `craft-anything--freebsd-x86_64.tar.gz` | ### Web (WebAssembly) | Build | File | Notes | |---|---|---| | Browser viewer | `craft-anything-web-.zip` | Says what a file is, in the browser (the file never leaves it); host the folder on any static web server ([packaging/web/README.md](packaging/web/README.md)) |

Come make things with us

Our Discord is where artists of every kind hang out: people who paint, shoot, draw, cut film, set type, and people still figuring out what they like to make. T3 Code

The open-source control plane for coding agents.

Download · iOS · Android · Web · Docs · Discord

T3 Code runs the coding agents on your machine and gives them one fast interface. Start a thread at your desk, then approve the next step from your phone. It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build, Antigravity, Kiro, Pi, Muse Code, fx, and any [ACP](./docs/user/providers-acp.md) agent. If an agent is set up on your computer, T3 Code can control it. ## What you get - **Your subscriptions.** T3 Code does not resell tokens. It drives the agents you are already signed in to. - **Every agent in one place.** Change models in the middle of a thread. Let Claude hand a task to Codex. - **Desktop, web, and phone.** One server, and every client shows the same threads. There are apps for iOS and Android. - **Remote ready.** Run agents on any machine. Connect over your local network, Tailscale, or [T3 Connect](./docs/user/remote-access.md). - **Git built in.** Each thread can work in its own worktree. Review the diff, then commit, push, and open a pull request with one button. - **Fast.** Performance is a feature here. We measure it, and we treat a dropped frame as a bug. - **Open.** MIT licensed. If you don't like something, fork it. ## Install ### Desktop app [Download T3 Code](https://t3.codes/download) for macOS, Windows, or Linux. You can also use a package manager: | Platform | Command | | -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | | macOS | `brew install --cask t3-code` | | Windows | `winget install T3Tools.T3Code` or `scoop install extras/t3code` | | Arch Linux | `yay -S t3code-bin` | | Nix | `nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code` | | Debian, Ubuntu | `.deb` from [Releases](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/releases) | ### Command line This installs the `t3` command. Run `t3` to start the server and open the web app. ```bash curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh ``` On Windows, in PowerShell: ```powershell irm https://t3.codes/install.ps1 | iex ``` To try it once without an install, run `npx t3@latest`. ### Phone Get the app from the [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/t3-code-remote-claude-more/id6787819824) or [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.t3tools.t3code). Then follow [remote access](./docs/user/remote-access.md) to connect it to your computer. ### Sign in to an agent T3 Code needs one agent that is installed and signed in. For example, install [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code) and run `claude auth login`, or install [Codex CLI](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli) and run `codex login`. [Provider setup](./docs/user/install.md#providers) has the steps for each agent. [Install T3 Code](./docs/user/install.md) covers nightly builds, AppImage, WSL, and NixOS. ## "Wait, what are you selling me?" Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar. We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the tool that you want. ## Documentation - [Install and first run](./docs/user/install.md) - [Remote access from a phone or another machine](./docs/user/remote-access.md) - [Permission modes](./docs/user/permission-modes.md) - [Source control](./docs/user/source-control.md) - [Connect outside agents over MCP](./docs/user/outside-agents.md) - [FAQ](./docs/user/faq.md) [All docs](./docs/README.md) has the full list. ## Contributing We have limited review capacity. Small, focused fixes are the most likely to be merged. Features need an approved discussion first. - Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) before you report a bug or open a pull request. - Put feature requests in [Ideas](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/discussions/categories/ideas). - Build from source with the [development runbook](./docs/operations/development.md#first-checkout). The [architecture overview](./docs/internals/overview.md) explains how it works. - Get help in [Discord](https://discord.gg/jn4EGJjrvv). ## License [MIT](./LICENSE)
